title: Base-b Divisibility Rules
description: Generalizes divisibility rules to arbitrary bases: for b ≥ 3, (b-1) | n iff (b-1) | digit_sum_b(n). Covers hexadecimal (mod 15), octal (mod 7), factor tests, and cross-base divisibility. All 15 theorems fully verified.

overview.historicalContext: Divisibility rules based on digit sums trace back to medieval Islamic mathematics: al-Khwārizmī (c. 825) described 'casting out nines' for verifying arithmetic. The method was widely transmitted to Europe via Fibonacci's *Liber Abaci* (1202). The underlying algebraic principle—that $b \equiv 1 \pmod{b-1}$ makes every positional digit-sum a modular invariant—was understood by Euler and Gauss in the 18th century as a consequence of modular arithmetic. This formalization generalizes the base-10 rule (parent proof) to arbitrary bases, revealing that 'casting out nines' is just one instance of a universal phenomenon: in any base $b$, digit sums determine remainders modulo $b-1$ and its factors. The cross-base theorem (Part VI) appears to be a novel formalization, connecting digit-sum tests across different bases.
overview.problemStatement:
**Base-b Divisibility Rules:**

For b ≥ 3 and n ∈ ℕ:
$$n \equiv \sum_i d_i \pmod{b-1}$$
where $d_i$ are the base-b digits of n.

More generally, for any d ≥ 2 dividing (b-1):
$$d \mid n \iff d \mid \sum_i d_i$$
overview.text: A 162-line formalization extending the parent base-10 divisibility rule to arbitrary bases, proving 15 theorems with 0 axioms and 0 sorries. The foundational insight is `base_mod_pred`: $b \bmod (b-1) = 1$ for $b \geq 3$, proved by Euclidean division. Since $b \equiv 1 \pmod{b-1}$, every power $b^k \equiv 1$, so $n = \sum d_i b^i \equiv \sum d_i \pmod{b-1}$. The `factor_mod` lemma extends this: if $d \mid (b-1)$ then $b \equiv 1 \pmod{d}$, yielding $d \mid n \iff d \mid \mathrm{digitsum}_b(n)$. Six concrete specializations cover hexadecimal (mod 15, 3, 5) and octal (mod 7), with `native_decide` verification on $\mathrm{0xFF}$, $\mathrm{0x100}$, and $\mathrm{0o777}$. The most novel result is `cross_base_divisibility`: if $d \mid (b_1 - 1)$ and $d \mid (b_2 - 1)$, then the digit-sum divisibility test by $d$ gives the same answer in both bases. Two consistency theorems confirm the general theory reproduces the parent proof's base-10 rules for 3 and 9.
overview.proofStrategy: The key observation is b ≡ 1 (mod b-1), proved by Euclidean division: b = (b-1)·1 + 1. Then b^k ≡ 1^k = 1 (mod b-1), so n = Σ dᵢ·b^i ≡ Σ dᵢ (mod b-1). For factors d of (b-1), the same logic applies since b ≡ 1 (mod d).
keyInsights: b % (b-1) = 1 is the universal principle behind all digit-sum divisibility tests
In hex: 16 ≡ 1 (mod 15), enabling mod-15, mod-5, and mod-3 tests
Cross-base: 3 | n can be tested via digit sums in base 10, 16, or any base where 3 | (b-1)
The formalization uses native_decide for computational verification, bridging abstract modular arithmetic with concrete number-theoretic examples

sections.title: Module Header, Imports, and Documentation
sections.summary: Imports Mathlib, documents the file's scope (generalizing divisibility rules to arbitrary bases), lists completed goals, and establishes the DivisibilityBy3OQ02 namespace. References Mathlib's `Nat.modEq_digits_sum` and `Nat.dvd_iff_dvd_digits_sum` as key dependencies.
sections.mathContext: The universal principle: $b \equiv 1 \pmod{b-1}$, so $n = \sum d_i b^i \equiv \sum d_i \pmod{b-1}$. This is the foundation of casting out 9s (base 10), 7s (base 8), 15s (base 16).

sections.title: Part I: Key Helper Lemmas
sections.summary: base_mod_pred (b % (b−1) = 1 for b ≥ 3) and factor_mod (b % d = 1 when d | (b−1)): the modular arithmetic foundations that enable all downstream divisibility rules.

sections.title: Part II: The Universal (b−1) Rule
sections.summary: Three equivalent forms of the (b−1) rule: congruence (n ≡ digitsum mod b−1), divisibility iff ((b−1) | n ↔ (b−1) | digitsum), and remainder equality (n mod (b−1) = digitsum mod (b−1)). All are one-line applications of Mathlib.

sections.title: Part III: Factor Divisibility
sections.summary: dvd_factor_iff: for any d ≥ 2 dividing (b−1), d | n ↔ d | digitsum_b(n). One theorem generating all classical digit-sum tests.

sections.title: Part IV: Specific Base Examples
sections.summary: Six concrete specializations: hex divisibility by 15, 3, 5; octal divisibility by 7; plus hex mod 15 and octal mod 7 remainder forms.
sections.mathContext: Base 16: $16 - 1 = 15 = 3 \times 5$, so digit sums test divisibility by 15, 3, and 5. Base 8: $8 - 1 = 7$, so digit sums test divisibility by 7.

sections.title: Part V: Numerical Verifications
sections.summary: Three native_decide examples: 15 | 255 (0xFF), 15 ∤ 256 (0x100), 7 | 511 (0o777). Bridges abstract proofs to concrete computation.
sections.mathContext: $255 = \mathrm{0xFF}$: hex digit sum $= 15 + 15 = 30$, $15 \mid 30$. $256 = \mathrm{0x100}$: hex digit sum $= 1$, $15 \nmid 1$.

sections.title: Part VI: Cross-Base Divisibility
sections.summary: cross_base_divisibility: if d | (b₁−1) and d | (b₂−1), digit-sum tests in either base are equivalent. Example: 3 | decimalsum(n) ↔ 3 | hexsum(n).

sections.title: Part VII: Parent Consistency
sections.summary: consistent_div3 and consistent_div9: confirms the general theory reproduces the parent proof's base-10 rules for 3 and 9 as special cases.
sections.mathContext: $3 \mid n \iff 3 \mid \mathrm{digitsum}_{10}(n)$ and $9 \mid n \iff 9 \mid \mathrm{digitsum}_{10}(n)$, recovered by instantiating $b = 10$ in the general theory.

conclusion.summary: Complete formalization of base-b divisibility rules with 0 axioms and 0 sorries. The universal principle b ≡ 1 (mod b-1) explains all digit-sum divisibility tests across all bases.
conclusion.implications: Programmers can use digit-sum tests in any base for quick divisibility checks. The cross-base theorem shows that divisibility by 3 can be checked equally well in decimal, hexadecimal, or any base ≡ 1 (mod 3).
openQuestions: Can the alternating digit sum rule (for b+1) be formalized? E.g., 11 | n ↔ alternating digit sum divisible by 11.
Can the theory extend to composite moduli not dividing (b−1)? E.g., divisibility by 7 in base 10 requires a weighted digit sum since 7 ∤ 9.
Is there a uniform formalization of Korselt's criterion connecting these digit-sum tests to Carmichael numbers?

crossReferences.description: Generalizes the parent base-10 divisibility-by-3 and divisibility-by-9 rules to arbitrary bases b ≥ 3, with consistency theorems confirming the general theory reproduces the parent's results
OQ-01 extends the base-10 divisibility rule in a different direction; this OQ-02 generalizes to arbitrary bases, while OQ-01 may explore other extensions

Both formalize modular arithmetic: CRT shows how to combine congruences mod coprime moduli, while the base-b divisibility rule uses the congruence b ≡ 1 (mod b−1) to transfer divisibility to digit sums

Truncation-based divisibility tests complement digit-sum tests: truncation works for divisors d where b ≡ 0 (mod d), while digit sums work when b ≡ 1 (mod d). Together they cover the two extreme cases of b mod d

Both connect number theory to modular arithmetic: Wilson's theorem characterizes primes via factorial congruences, while digit-sum rules characterize divisibility via positional representation congruences
